articles.title: 2026 Bowl Predictions and Updated Playoff Bracket Projections After Week 12 Rankings
articles.summary: It wouldn't be entirely accurate to say that Week 11 was an uneventful one in the world of college football. However, we didn't see any major upsets involving top-ranked teams, and we didn't see any major shakeups in the latest College Football Playoff (CFP) rankings, which were released on Tuesday evening.
articles.body:
It wouldn't be entirely accurate to say that Week 11 was an uneventful one in the world of college football. However, we didn't see any major upsets involving top-ranked teams, and we didn't see any major shakeups in the latest College Football Playoff (CFP) rankings, which were released on Tuesday evening.

What we did see was a few CFP hopefuls having their playoff chances essentially squashed. LSU, for example, nearly kept its title dreams alive but lost at the last second when Arch Manning delivered a game-winning touchdown strike to give Texas the win.

Kentucky also faltered, losing a 21-14 contest against Florida and falling from the ranks of the true contenders in the process.

Wake Forest stayed in the playoff hunt with a 49-7 blowout win over SMU, while Boise State outlasted Oregon State to remain the top Group of Six contender.

Here, we'll dive into the latest CFP rankings, preview Week 12, and make some predictions for the CFP's biggest bowl games and final bracket.

Week 12 won't bring any major matchups between top CFP contenders. However, there will be a few important games for those on the fringes of the playoff field.

Tennessee, for example, must outlast LSU in order to stay within the top 12. The Tigers will undoubtedly be motivated after allowing their CFP chances against Texas, so this will be a dangerous game for Josh Heupel's squad.

Texas Tech is another fringe team and will have to outlast Baylor to have a shot at sneaking into the playoff. Wake Forest will have to beat Georgia Tech, though the Demon Deacons' playoff chances will most likely hinge on an anticipated ACC title game matchup with Miami on December 5.

Of course, if Wake Forest doesn't win out, it may not have a shot at the ACC Championship.

Top-ranked teams will also need to avoid potential traps in Week 12. Georgia, for example, must take care of business against a quality South Carolina squad on Saturday. UCLA must handle a Big-Ten matchup with Michigan, while Utah will need to outlast TCU.

Barring any significant surprises, though, the rankings are unlikely to look much different a week from now.

CFP Bowl and Bracket Predictions Entering Week 12

While Week 12 might not heavily impact the playoff race, looming conference championships will. The four power conferences will send their champions to the CFP via automatic bids, which is why earning spots in those games is critical.

The top G6 champion will also earn an automatic bid, likely to be the No. 12 spot. Along with Boise State, Liberty and Louisiana Tech have already secured spots in their conference championship games.

Notre Dame is also guaranteed a spot in the CFP if the Irish finish with a top-12 ranking. This will eliminate the possibility of Notre Dame being bumped for a G6 school like Boise State if the Irish finish in that 12th position. Right now, that's an irrelevant factor.

Byes will not be automatically awarded to the top conference champions, as was the case a couple of years ago. This is why we could see two schools from the same conference earn byes, even if they meet in the conference title game.

The prediction here is that Georgia will narrowly defeat Alabama in the last SEC Championship for the foreseeable future, leaving both teams as top-four squads in the eyes of the committee.

Utah and UCLA are both undefeated and should earn top-four spots if they remain undefeated and win the Big 12 and Big Ten, respectively.

articles.title: Dundee boss Steven Pressley calls for national centre to enhance Scottish game
articles.summary: Scotland would benefit from the creation of a national football centre, argues Dundee head coach Steven Pressley, who likens the current structure of the game to building on sand.
articles.body:
Scotland would benefit from the creation of a national football centre, argues Dundee head coach Steven Pressley, who likens the current structure of the game to building on sand.

The health of Scottish football is under the spotlight once more following a poor Nations League campaign under new head coach Sebastien Pocognoli, continued club struggles in Europe and concern over the lack of game time for homegrown talent in the Premiership.

"We have to look at it as more of our game as a whole," said Pressley, who was capped 32 times for Scotland.

"There is a lot of talk about how we get our young players playing and more minutes and there are so many opinions around this.

"I want to get behind something. We don't have our own national football facility.

"I went to Hungary with Dundee in the summer and we stayed at their national centre, it was an outstanding facility with terrific pitches, classrooms, seminar rooms, areas for everybody to progress, areas for everybody to connect.

"When I look at our own country just now I think how do we improve all of our coaches, how do we improve all our young players, how do we improve our analysis, how do we improve our sports science, how do we improve our leadership when we don't even have a facility that we can all come together and really move the country forwards?

"Just now I see us trying to build our country on sand and I mean that, we need a foundation where we can finally grow from. Something that we are proud of."

In England, there is St George's Park - a £105m national football centre of excellence, which opened in 2012.

The Scottish FA instead uses facilities at the Oriam Sports Performance Centre in Edinburgh and at Lesser Hampden.

They also sporadically use the Sportscotland National Sports Training centre in Largs, as well as facilities at Ravenscraig and Toryglen.

"For us as a country, a top-50 ranked country, not to have that type of facility worries me," added Pressley, who captained Hearts and played for Rangers, Celtic and Dundee United.

"It says a lot about our strategy, our longevity and our long-term vision and we are finally seeing the effects of that. We have shown none of that over the period and it is all horribly catching up with us.

"We need to start with the absolute basics of a facility that we can start to go from, a lot of the other things will come with time but we always want to fix the here and now rather than saying 'OK we need to build something special'.

"As a result of that, we would see great improvements in so many different areas.

"We would see coaches coming together sharing ideas. When I have done things like my university course and my diploma in football management, I did them at St George's Park.

"We all came together there, we all improved our education there. We need to do that in our own country, make our country proud again and really help each other."

articles.title: USMNT vs. Mexico and Updated Bracket, Schedule for 2026-27 Concacaf Nations League
articles.summary: The United States Men's National Soccer Team will have to get through its biggest rival in order to reach the finals of the 2026-27 CONCACAF Nations League.
articles.body:
The United States Men's National Soccer Team will have to get through its biggest rival in order to reach the finals of the 2026-27 CONCACAF Nations League.

Following the United States' 2-0 win over Haiti and Mexico's 1-0 victory against Jamaica in the Nations League quarterfinals on Tuesday, it has been confirmed that the U.S. and Mexico will clash in the semifinals on March 25:

Canada and Panama will meet in the other semifinal with the winner of that match facing the winner of the United States vs. Mexico in the 2026-27 CONCACAF Nations League final on March 28 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

The CONCACAF Nations League has a two-legged quarterfinal, and the United States had no problem crushing Haiti 8-0 on aggregate, including a 2-0 triumph in the second leg on Tuesday.

There was some added emotion behind the victory since it marked Mauricio Pochettino's final match as head coach of the USMNT after accepting the managerial job at Manchester United.

Mexico unexpectedly had a much tougher time advancing, needing to overcome a 3-2 loss to Jamaica in the first leg. The Mexicans rebounded with a 1-0 win on Tuesday, which was enough to tie the aggregate 3-3 and advance on away goals.

The United States, Mexico, Canada and Panama all automatically advanced to the quarterfinals of the Nations League as the top four seeds.

While Mexico and the U.S. were the top two seeds, they will have to face off in the semis due to the fact that the four quarterfinal winners were re-seeded based on their margin of victory.

Since the United States crushed Haiti 8-0 and Mexico barely scraped past Jamaica on away goals, they were effectively re-seeded as No. 1 and No. 4, respectively.

That means the Americans will have a tough road to their fourth Nations League title since the inception of the event in 2019.

The USMNT won the first three Nations League titles before Mexico won it in 2025, as the United States failed to reach the final and fell to Canada in the third-place game that year.

Despite their dominance in the quarterfinals, there is a great deal of uncertainty surrounding the USMNT entering the semifinals due to Pochettino's departure.

The United States figures to have a new head coach in place by the time the Nations League resumes about four months from now in March, but whether that coach can achieve instant success is anyone's guess.

articles.title: 'Our industry right now is laundering money' — With college sports in chaos, is a rev-share cap solution on the way?
articles.summary: A proposal from the SEC to impose financial penalties on schools for exceeding the athlete revenue-share cap is gaining traction across the four power league...
articles.body:
ARLINGTON, Va. — Each November, in or around the nation's capital, the Knight Commission holds an annual public meeting to discuss the state of college athletics.

Current and former college sports administrators and stakeholders gather in a room for about 90 minutes of conversations that, without failure, produce a jarring comment — or three.

With the industry at its most turbulent, this year's meeting did not disappoint.

The commissioner of the Ivy League suggested that high-resourced football programs should separate from the rest of Division I as "standalone, for-profit ventures"; an FCS athletic director turned his ire on the professional leagues to relax their eligibility rules, such as the NFL requiring high school players to spend three years in college; and, perhaps most notable of all, a recently retired power conference athletic director said the real quiet part aloud.

"Our industry right now is laundering money," said former Iowa State athletic director Jamie Pollard, one of the speakers at Tuesday's gathering in this Washington, D.C. suburb.

A stunning comment from such a recent high-profile figure, Pollard's description is one that many top school and conference officials have privately espoused to characterize the athlete compensation landscape: Schools are redirecting booster, sponsor and apparel money from the athletic department to their rosters disguised as marketing and endorsement deals in an effort to circumvent the enforcement operation.

However, as Pollard and other stakeholders here spoke, the gears churned behind the scenes to bring sweeping changes to the much-maligned system.

A proposal from the SEC to impose financial penalties on schools for exceeding the athlete revenue-share cap is gaining traction not only within the conference but across the four power leagues, those with knowledge of the discussion tell Yahoo Sports.

According to the proposal — reported in detail last week — schools spending more than the $21.6 million revenue-share cap stand to be assessed millions in penalties in a concept most similar to pro sports-style luxury tax structures. For instance, according to one model circulated, those spending $70.5 million would owe a tax of roughly $14 million — an amount that would increase significantly beyond that figure.

While the plan originated from the SEC, leaders in the other power conferences — the Big Ten, ACC and Big 12 — are coalescing around the concept to the point of adopting it soon and, perhaps, communicating their plans with the co-lead plaintiff attorneys in the House settlement, Jeffrey Kessler and Steve Berman. Both attorneys have suggested that such a cap policy may unnecessarily restrict athlete pay and have expressed doubt that it is legal without their approval under the House settlement — the NCAA's multi-billion dollar agreement that governs the industry's new athlete compensation system.

During and after the Knight Commission meeting, Anil Gollahalli, the Big Ten's chief legal officer and general counsel, discussed the Big Ten's own cap policy — passed last month — and the one circulated from the SEC. He said the two are "distinctly different." The Big Ten's rule only applies to those within the league, while the SEC's proposal — possibly now embraced by all power conferences and administered by the College Sports Commission — may necessitate crossing other legal hurdles.

"You have to draw a distinction about what conferences can do by themselves versus what leagues can do collectively and perhaps in connection with [House plaintiff attorneys]," Gollahalli told Yahoo Sports. "I can't comment on what the right mechanisms are because I don't know what the contours of the proposal will finally end up being."

Described as a "Plan B" if Congress does not pass federal legislation to regulate the industry — seemingly a longshot at this point — the cap policy circulated by the SEC features a tiered system of gradually increasing fines for those exceeding the revenue-share cap. Fines would begin at less than 1% of overages for those spending $22-$50.5 million on their rosters, and then increase to 1% for those spending $50.5-60.5 million, then to 3% for those spending $60.5-70.5 million and, finally, to 10% for those spending more than $70.5 million.

However, penalty figure amounts continue to be an ongoing conversation among administrators and are subject to change.

The cap policy's intent is clear: slow spending by charging schools additional revenue. But some of the richest programs in the country — i.e. Texas, Ohio State, Miami, etc. — may continue to lap the college football spending field despite the penalty.

"They'll just pay the fine," says one major conference athletic director.

Money was at the center of Tuesday's Knight Commission meeting. At the top level of major college football, schools are believed to be spending more than $40 million on their football rosters and some exceeding more than $15 million for men's basketball.

University officials are in the midst of negotiations to land high school prospects, re-sign their current players and target potential transfers in a hotly competitive recruiting market that is expected to increase by as much or more than 30% during this cycle.

To that end, on Tuesday, Ivy League commissioner Robin Harris made a somewhat bold and revolutionary statement: Perhaps those rich football powers should go do their own thing.

"Call a spade a spade," Harris told Yahoo Sports. "They are operating as revenue-producing entities for profit. And they are paying athletes a lot of money and paying coaches a lot of money. It should be a standalone, but yet affiliated, for-profit venture. They are operated as taxable entities but are still affiliated with the institutions. You have to have a different structure and rules. What that looks like, I don't know."

She is perhaps referencing the long-discussed split of the power leagues, or perhaps even a smaller group of high-revenue producing football programs. A split into a "semi-pro model" would bring "reality and rational choices" to the schools outside of those leagues that are "overspending and can't afford it," she said.

"They are chasing something that they cannot obtain," Harris said. "Now they would free up dollars to be put to the greater good."

But even those in the power leagues are struggling to keep pace with their blue-blood brethren, says Pollard. He condemned college leaders for making short-term decisions that have "long-term consequences" and believes that university presidents and their boards are making "irrational and emotional" decisions in shifting campus funds to athletics where they are "no way going to be repaid."

College leaders are taking out loans for athletics to be paid back with revenue from new television deals, he says. But he does not believe some of those new media deals — such as one in his former conference, the Big 12 — will be lucrative enough to pay back those loans.

"I come from a conference that as late as two years ago our commissioner told our board, 'If I can't get you 2.5 times in 2031 [the value] from our television deal, I should be fired,'" Pollard said.

"We'll be lucky to get 1 times," he said. "Think about that. We're making decisions today about revenue in the future that's most likely not going to be there."

But perhaps the money-washing that Pollard referenced in his opening comments Tuesday may subside with a new cap policy.

The concept would consider some school-affiliated, third-party NIL deals as "institutional pay," such as a redirecting of revenues from corporate sponsors, multi-media rights partners and perhaps even apparel brands. This would remove the requirement for schools to gain approval from the College Sports Commission's NIL Go clearinghouse for NIL agreements with such entities — what is now a time-consuming and resource-draining measure to circumvent the existing cap by paying as much as 20% to third-party entities to "wash money," as officials describe it.

But college executives believe a cap policy would not be necessary if Congress would pass the Protect College Sports Act, the all-encompassing college sports bill that overwhelmingly passed the Senate but faces a stiff test in the House of Representatives.

Steve Eigenbrot, a former South Carolina administrator who is the athletic director at FCS Towson, offered a different suggestion for the congressional lobbying effort. He believes the federal government should examine professional league-eligibility rules that prevent high school or early college athletes from earning compensation at the NFL level.

"Maurice Clarett famously won a court case and then he didn't," he said of the former Ohio State running back who was denied early entrance in the NFL. "Had that moment changed, I think we would be looking at this problem very differently."

One of the NCAA's senior vice presidents, Tim Buckley, told the Knight Commission on Tuesday that the NCAA is "the closest we've ever been" to having legislation passed. And while that's true, many view it as a longshot in a House chamber that may run out of time before a new Congress arrives in January. There are only three more full working weeks remaining in the congressional calendar.

For the legislation to pass the House in a "traditional way," it is "highly unlikely to get to the finish line" because of the calendar, said Rob Mangus, a subject-matter expert for the Knight Commission who gave an update on the bill Tuesday.

"There just isn't enough time to do it," he told the room. "Is there going to be a vote at all? Some people think not."

articles.title: El Bournemouth se pone en órbita
articles.standfirst: La racha de ocho victorias mejora el juego del equipo, aunque el marcador la exagera, sobre todo en defensa
articles.summary: La racha de ocho victorias mejora el juego del equipo, aunque el marcador la exagera, sobre todo en defensa
articles.body: El 10 de octubre, el Bournemouth salió de Stamford Bridge con un 5-1 en contra, el puesto 18 de la Premier y tres puntos en seis jornadas. Marco Rose llevaba seis partidos de liga en el banquillo y las dudas sobre su futuro ya circulaban. La herencia era exigente. Andoni Iraola anunció el 15 de abril que dejaría el club al terminar la temporada y el Bournemouth confirmó poco después a Rose, con contrato hasta 2029, un técnico al que el RB Leipzig había destituido en marzo. Su antecesor había consolidado al equipo en la Premier durante tres temporadas y lo dejó con 13 partidos sin perder al final del curso. Ocho victorias consecutivas después, el cohete ha despegado, el equipo es séptimo con 15 puntos y la racha ya tiene explicaciones para todos los gustos. Que si la defensa, que si el calendario, que si Evanilson. Los datos permiten ordenarlas. Los números ya decían que aquel arranque era mejor que la tabla. Según Opta acumulaba 8,4 puntos esperados tras seis jornadas, frente a los 3 reales, es decir, estaba sumando menos puntos de los que debería. Además, acumuló ocasiones de mejor calidad en cuatro de esos seis partidos (ante Everton, Newcastle, Brentford y Chelsea). Solo contra City y Liverpool fue al revés, los dos partidos en los que el resultado y el juego coincidieron. Rose lo veía igual: "En cuanto a rendimiento, veo muchas cosas buenas", decía tras los primeros tropiezos. El caso extremo es Stamford Bridge. El Chelsea marcó cinco goles con 1,09 xG, un acierto que por probabilidad se da una de cada doscientas veces, mientras el Bournemouth generaba 1,38. Hasta ahí, mala suerte. Rose no lo escondió: "Nos han dado una bofetada de verdad y ahora tenemos que reaccionar", dijo antes de recibir al Sturm Graz en Europa League. Pero la suerte no explica ocho victorias seguidas, y por eso conviene mirar qué ha pasado después. Si se comparan las seis primeras jornadas con las cuatro últimas, la diferencia de goles esperados por partido pasa de 0,01 a 1,68. A primera vista, el ataque explicaría cerca del 70 % de ese salto, con un xG a favor que sube de 1,35 a 2,52 por partido. Pero esos datos los deforman un solo partido, el del Sunderland, que se quedó con diez desde el minuto 17 y recibió 4,23 xG del Bournemouth. Sin ese encuentro, que pudo ser un atípico, el equipo genera 1,95 por partido y concede 0,83 sin contar penaltis, frente a 1,35 y 1,34 en el arranque. La mejora sigue ahí, aunque más pequeña (la diferencia de xG queda en 1,12) y repartida casi a medias entre el ataque (0,60) y la defensa (0,51). El volumen de tiros cuenta lo mismo. De los 65 que firmó en las cuatro últimas jornadas, 29 llegaron ante ese Sunderland con diez. Sin él quedan 12 por partido, menos que los 12,8 del arranque, pero a 0,16 xG por tiro en lugar de 0,11. Los mapas de Opta lo dejan ver, porque en las seis primeras jornadas buena parte de los remates salían desde fuera del área y en las cuatro últimas la mancha se ha mudado dentro. La defensa es donde se marca la real diferencia. Concede casi los mismos tiros que antes, 10 por partido frente a 10,7, aunque de peor calidad. Y sin embargo los goles en contra bajan de 2,17 a 0,25 por partido, una caída casi cuatro veces mayor que la del xG en contra (de 1,34 a 0,84). En las cuatro últimas jornadas solo encajó un gol, de penalti, con 3,36 xG en contra acumulados. Nada cambia si contamos también los partidos que, entre medias, ha jugado en otras competiciones como la Carabao Cup o la Europa League. En siete de los ocho partidos (sin datos del Carabao ante el Villa) el Bournemouth concedió 5,9 xG, con el penalti de Ipswich incluido, y encajó dos goles. Con una aproximación estadística básica, una distancia así ocurre una de cada quince veces. Europa deja una pista parecida. En Praga, el Sparta ganó el duelo de xG (2,09 a 1,43) y el Bournemouth se llevó el partido por 1-3. ¿Qué ha cambiado, entonces, en la pizarra? Según las posiciones medias en nueve de los diez partidos de liga, casi nada. Petrović, Truffert, Silva, Hill, Smith, Tavernier, Rayan y Evanilson abrieron los nueve, con Tavernier por la izquierda y Rayan por la derecha. Solo en Stamford Bridge, sin Scott, Kluivert ni Kroupi, Rayan acabó más cerca de la izquierda que de la derecha. El cambio está en el interior. Scott, titular en los primeros partidos y habitual por el interior izquierdo, se cayó en los cinco últimos. Christie ha empezado cinco de los últimos seis y Kluivert, titular en tres de los cuatro últimos, se coloca más a la derecha que en las primeras jornadas. Hasta el 10 de octubre, día de la última derrota, el 40,9 % de los toques de ataque del Bournemouth se producía por la izquierda y el 32,0 % por la derecha. Desde el 11 de octubre la izquierda baja al 31,7 % y la derecha sube al 40,6 %. El relevo de un interior izquierdo por otro más centrado y el mayor peso de Kluivert por la derecha encajan con ese giro, aunque con cuatro partidos de muestra no pasa de hipótesis. Sin balón, la continuidad también es la regla. El Bournemouth es el cuarto de la Premier por la distancia a la que empiezan sus secuencias de presión (43,5 metros) y segundo en recuperaciones altas (93). Lo llamativo es que 20 de ellas acaban en tiro, el 21,5 %, la sexta cifra más alta, con el noveno PPDA (11,4) de la competición. Evanilson ha marcado en cinco jornadas seguidas de liga, algo que ningún jugador del club había hecho antes, y esta vez los datos acompañan a los goles. En las cuatro últimas jornadas acumula 3,78 xG sin penaltis, 0,95 por partido, frente a los 1,54 de las seis primeras (0,26 por partido). Sus tiros sin bloqueos pasan de 1,7 a 4,5 cada 90 minutos y sus toques en el área rival, de 3,3 a 7,3. Rose se lo pidió tras el gol de Ipswich: "Espero que siga hambriento, porque será bueno para nosotros". El delantero ha pasado de generar el 19% del xG del equipo al 37% y explica por sí solo en torno al 60% de la mejora ofensiva por partido, con el Sunderland dentro del cálculo, de modo que es un orden de magnitud. El dato encaja con el relevo del interior, ya que con Christie y Kluivert el 9 recibe el doble de balones en el área, aunque los materiales no permiten atribuirlo todavía a esos cambios. Más llamativo en eficiencia es Tavernier, con 2,02 xG sin penaltis en cuatro jornadas y 0,34 xG por tiro, el mejor registro de la liga entre quienes han hecho al menos cinco remates, una cifra que rara vez se mantiene. Rose, preguntado por si Tuchel había ido a ver a Tavernier, bromeó con que "quizá no consiguió entrada porque nuestro estadio es un poco más pequeño". En todo esto influye también el calendario. Los seis primeros rivales de liga del Bournemouth fueron muchos de los considerados grandes y, entre los seis suman 97 puntos tras diez jornadas, 16,2 de media. Los cuatro últimos, 41, con una media de 10,3. El Sunderland jugó con diez desde el minuto 17 y el Leeds regaló el primer gol por un error de su portero. El matiz honesto es que el equipo ya se había medido con City, Newcastle, Liverpool y Chelsea en el arranque, y el juego estaba mejor de lo que decían los puntos. Cuatro partidos de liga apenas dan para una señal. Hacen falta más encuentro (y por tanto, datos) para saber si este cambio es realmente sostenible. Si aguantan, Rose habrá corregido algo más que la mala suerte de agosto. Si no, el Bournemouth habrá vivido un mes en el que, por una vez, el marcador se puso de su parte.

articles.title: Emma Hayes names USWNT World Cup qualifying roster with 4 NWSL finalists including Trinity Rodman
articles.summary: Four players preparing for Saturday's NWSL championship will have a quick turnaround before next week's World Cup qualifying match against El Salvador.
articles.body:
Soon after expected major roles in the National Women's Soccer League championship match this weekend, four players will need to pivot quickly to the U.S. national team and World Cup qualifying.

In an announcement Wednesday, U.S. coach Emma Hayes' 23-member roster included two players from each of the NWSL finalists: Washington Spirit forward Trinity Rodman and defender Tara Rudd and Kansas City Current midfielder Croix Bethune and forward Michelle Cooper.

Hayes is expected to attend the NWSL final at Washington's Audi Field on Saturday night — two days before camp opens in the Dallas area.

Doubling as the 2027 World Cup and 2028 Olympic qualifying tournament, the CONCACAF W Championship will commence Nov. 27 in Mansfield, Texas. The Dec. 1 semifinals will also take place in Mansfield, and the Dec. 5 final is scheduled for Houston's Shell Energy Stadium.

Ranked No. 2 in the world, the Americans will need only to defeat No. 78 El Salvador in the quarterfinals to secure their 10th consecutive World Cup appearance. Even if the Salvadorans pull off a historic upset, a backdoor into next summer's competition in Brazil is available.

As Olympic host, the U.S. received an automatic berth and will seek to defend its 2024 gold medal.

The other quarterfinals will pit Jamaica (ranked 40th) vs. Costa Rica (41), Canada (9) vs. Panama (54), and Mexico (28) vs. Haiti (48).

"It's been a great year of growth and learning for our team, and for a long time the focus has been on qualifying for the World Cup, so now that time has arrived," Hayes said. "I want to see relentless consistency from our players, individually and as a team, and I want us to be elite in both penalty boxes. If we can achieve that, I'm confident those performances will carry us through to meet our standards and goals. This is my first Concacaf event and the first for many of our players, so we're all looking forward to the experience."

The CONCACAF tournament will mark the return of midfielders Sam Coffey and Bethune, who missed the two friendlies against top-ranked Spain last month because of injuries. Naomi Girma, the star center back, remains unavailable with a muscle injury.

Angel City FC left back Evelyn Shores, who received her first U.S. call-up last month but didn't play, is the second player in program history to make a World Cup qualifying roster without any senior experience.

Bethune, who set the NWSL single-season record for assists with 11, was last in U.S. camp in June but hasn't made an appearance since January.

Coffey, from Manchester City, is among four players from European clubs involved in the UEFA Champions League. The others are OL Lyonnes midfielder Lily Yohannes, Chelsea winger Alyssa Thompson and Arsenal right back Emily Fox.

Goalkeepers : Claudia Dickey (Seattle Reign), Mandy McGlynn (Utah Royals), Phallon Tullis-Joyce (Manchester United).

Defenders : Tierna Davidson (Gotham FC), Kate Del Fava (Utah Royals), Emily Fox (Arsenal), Avery Patterson (Houston Dash), Tara Rudd (Washington Spirit), Evelyn Shores (Angel City), Gisele Thompson (Angel City), Kennedy Wesley (San Diego Wave).

Midfielders : Croix Bethune (Kansas City Current), Sam Coffey (Manchester City), Lindsey Heaps (Denver Summit), Claire Hutton (Bay FC), Rose Lavelle (Gotham FC), Lily Yohannes (OL Lyonnes).

Forwards : Michelle Cooper (Kansas City Current), Trinity Rodman (Washington Spirit), Ashley Sanchez (North Carolina Courage), Mallory Swanson (Chicago Stars), Alyssa Thompson (Chelsea FC), Sophia Wilson (Portland Thorns).

articles.title: 'Best night' of Dáithí Mac Gabhann's life all thanks to organ donation
articles.summary: Dáithí Mac Gabhann walked out with Republic of Ireland's Troy Parrott as Ireland won 3-0 over Kosovo in the Nations League.
articles.body:
A 10-year-old boy who inspired changes to Northern Ireland's organ donation laws "skipped" onto the pitch as a mascot at the Republic of Ireland match on Tuesday evening.

It was "the best night of his life" and is something he would not have been able to do without the gift of a new heart, his father Máirtín said.

Dáithí Mac Gabhann received a transplant in July after an eight-year wait, and his father said he is "doing incredible" and "living his life to the absolute fullest".

Dáithí walked out with Republic of Ireland's Troy Parrott as Ireland won 3-0 over Kosovo in the Nations League , with Parrott having scored two of the goals.

It wasn't the first time Dáithí has been a mascot. A couple of years ago he walked out with Toni Leigh Finnegan for the Women's Irish Cup final with Cliftonville and Glentoran.

However, Finnegan had to carry him out as he required a wheelchair at the time.

"He had such an amazing experience, but this time he skipped out, and he skipped out simply because of the gift of organ donation, and how incredible the gift of organ donation is," Máirtín told BBC News NI.

"So he skipped out with Troy Parrott, wasn't out of breath once, sang as loud as he could, and was just absolutely full of beans the whole night, and he no way, not a chance, would he have been able to walk out that far had he not received the gift of a heart transplant."

Máirtín said his experience has "created a bit of a monster" as on Wednesday morning Dáithí was "outright refusing" to wear his uniform to school or wash his hands, as Troy Parrott had held them.

"So he's away into school with unwashed hands and in his Ireland kit from last night and I've never been happier for him to put his foot down and say, 'I'm not wearing a uniform today'."

Dáithí was born in 2016 with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, meaning that side of his heart did not form correctly.

In 2023 a law was introduced in Northern Ireland which means that people automatically become potential organ donors unless they explicitly say they wish not to be.

The legislation - officially the Organ and Tissue Donation (Deemed Consent) Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 - was known as Dáithí's Law, after his family spent years campaigning on the issue.

His many years of campaigning for a change to organ donation laws first caught the attention of the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) when he was two-years-old.

However, the journey down to Dublin for the match on Tuesday wasn't smooth sailing as the Dublin Port Tunnel was closed and the family were worried they would miss the start.

So much was the scurry that Máirtín had to stay behind for the initial walk out onto the pitch and Dáithí's grandad brought him in.

"I have never been so happy to have missed Dáithí walking out in front of 50,000 people with Troy Parrott, because it meant he made it," he said.

"I was screaming in the car when I saw the photo because I was just so happy, I obviously would have loved to have been there, but it didn't matter anymore, it was as if Ireland scored the winner in the 90th minute.

"But I also said to Dáithí this is a lesson to you - why you never ever give up, because we shouldn't have made it in time, I just said we're not giving up here, so we're going to keep trying."

articles.title: The tightest Premier League survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry for Man Utd, Sunderland and Crystal Palace
articles.summary: The Premier League resumes on Saturday with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Man Utd in the relegation zone. But is it too early to be worried?
articles.body:
Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.

But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.

Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United , will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.

Sunderland , sandwiching the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.

But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.

The bottom three may already be taking shape

Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.

In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.

For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.

Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.

That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.

Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.

This is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.

They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.

The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.

This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.

Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.

Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.

While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.

Palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.

Sunderland 's eight points is also the most the side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.

In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven – the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.

The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for United next season.

Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.

Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.

That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.

The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.

The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.

As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.

That season West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.

Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.

articles.title: Real Madrid - Inter en directo | Última hora de Champions League Femenina en vivo hoy
articles.summary: También sabemos las once elegidas por parte del Inter de Milán: Rúnarsdóttir; Kullberg, Ivana Andrés, Milinkovic, Bartoli; Glionna, Santi, Vilhjálmsdó
articles.body:
Última hora del Real Madrid - Inter en directo:

¡¡¡Muuuy buenas tardes y bienvenidos a todos y todas a la quinta jornada de la Champions League femenina!!! Real Madrid e Inter se ven las caras en el Alfredo Di Stéfano en un partido en el que las madridistas intentarán ganar para auparse a los puestos de arriba de la tabla e intentar mantener sus opciones de clasificación directa a la siguiente fase.

El Real Madrid no conoce la derrota en los primeros cuatro partidos, y viene de estrenar el casillero de victorias en el último encuentro ante el Paris FC (3-0) , que colocó a las de Pau Quesada en séptimo lugar con seis puntos, a dos de los puestos de pase directo.

Enfrente, un Inter que está decimotercero con cuatro puntos. Después de estrenarse con victoria ante el Häcken (1-0), acumula un empate y dos derrotas que las colocan fuera de la zona de 'playoff'. A domicilio, firmó tablas ante el colista Austria Wien (1-1) y se llevó una goleada de Lyon (6-0).

Desde las 18.45 horas , el Real Madrid recibe al Inter en un gran partido de la Champions League femenina , y nosotros lo viviremos como siempre, aquí, en MARCA .

articles.title: Urban Meyer reportedly 'seriously considering' Maryland job after speaking with school's athletic director
articles.summary: Is Urban Meyer truly inching toward a return to college football?
articles.body:
Former Florida and Ohio State head coach Urban Meyer could be inching closer to a return to college football. Meyer is reportedly " seriously considering " the head coaching job at Maryland after meeting with the school's athletic director, according to InsideMDSports.com.

If Meyer took the job, it would mark the first time he's coached since 2021, when he was fired after just 13 games with the Jacksonville Jaguars. Prior to that, his last coaching job came with Ohio State, which he left after leading the team to a 12-1 record in 2018.

Given his success at the college ranks — he's won three national championships and is already in the College Football Hall of Fame — Meyer would undoubtedly be a significant hire for Maryland.

Whether Meyer's interest is sincere is the bigger question. The former coach has spoken openly about being considered for premier college football jobs in the past when his name was floated.

He's fielded rumors suggesting he was considering both Penn State and a return to Florida in recent years, but shut those down . While discussing the Penn State rumors last year, the 62-year-old Meyer flat out said he has "no interest in coaching again."

Since the end of his stint with the Jaguars, Meyer has served as a college football analyst at Fox Sports. He reportedly is "happy" with that role, per InsideMDSports.com, perhaps a sign Meyer will decide against a return to coaching.

If there's a reason to believe this time around will be different, it's that Meyer has pre-established relationships with a few important people at Maryland. Both Maryland athletic director Jim Smith and deputy athletic director Diana Sabau overlapped with Meyer at Ohio State, per InsideMDSports.com. Smith ran the program's alumni association at the time; Sabau was an associate athletic director at Ohio State.

That ultimately doesn't mean much. Given Meyer's status in the game and his longevity at premier college programs, he's bound to have connections at nearly every major football program.

Whether Meyer truly wants to return to college football is ultimately up to him. He's been content in recent years to discuss rumors, but hasn't seemed moved to return to coaching any time soon.

The Maryland job rumors could go down the same trajectory unless Meyer has experienced a change of heart since last November.

articles.title: El Manchester United estudia acciones legales por la salida de JJ Gabriel
articles.standfirst: Según 'The Times', analiza si algún club contactó con él este verano y se saltó la norma FIFA al respecto de jugadores menores de edad.
articles.summary: Según 'The Times', analiza si algún club contactó con él este verano y se saltó la norma FIFA al respecto de jugadores menores de edad.
articles.body: El Manchester United medita emprender acciones legales si encuentran pruebas de que JJ Gabriel fue sondeado por clubes de forma ilegal. El jugador de 16 años confirmó este martes que abandona el Manchester United y todo apunta a que en las próximas semanas firmará un contrato con el Real Madrid. De hecho hoy mismo ha visitado Valdebebas, como ha adelantado MARCA. Según el diario británico The Times, el United está estudiando si algún club contactó con JJ Gabriel este verano y se saltó las normas de la FIFA al respecto de jugadores menores de edad. Con la regulación actual, una vez se complete el fichaje por el Real Madrid, el United solo recibirá cerca de 300 000 libras en concepto de formación del jugador, una cifra que se aleja mucho de lo que podrían haber ingresado en un traspaso en el futuro. El club inglés está molesto por la actitud del jugador y su familia, que tras seis años en la entidad decidió forzar su salida y dejar de entrenar en Carrington, la ciudad deportiva del United. Esto ocurrió apenas unos días después de que anotara un 'hat trick' en la Youth League y planeara ser convocado al partido de Copa de la Liga del United contra el Brighton & Hove Albion. El United sostiene que no ha podido comunicarse con la familia del futbolista desde septiembre. JJ Gabriel no ha llegado a debutar con el United en partido oficial, aunque sí ha entrenado con el primer equipo y jugó unos minutos en un amistoso en verano. El caso es que tan sólo falta que el Madrid haga oficial el fichaje del joven una vez que el jugador se desvinculó ayer del Manchester United. En Inglaterra se tiran de los pelos por la marcha del joven atacante, y visto lo visto tratan de sacar tajada con el considerado mejor promesa surgida en el país en los últimos lustros. La presencia de Gabriel, que lleva varias semanas entrenando en solitario en España a la espera de la confirmación de su fichaje por el Real Madrid, ha despertado gran expectación en la Ciudad Deportiva del club blanco, donde no son ajenos al gran revuelo mediático que ha rodeado tanto la salida del futbolista del United como su llegada al club blanco.

articles.title: DJ Jacobs, Mark Matthews Headline 247 Sports' Updated CFB Recruiting Class Rankings for 2027
articles.summary: DJ Jacobs and Mark Matthews top the latest list of the top prospects in the 2027 college football recruiting class from 247Sports.
articles.body:
DJ Jacobs and Mark Matthews top the latest list of the top prospects in the 2027 college football recruiting class from 247Sports .

Here's a look at the top 25 from the updated rankings:

DJ Jacobs, EDGE, committed to Ohio State

Maxwell Hiller, IOL, committed to Florida

Jalen Brewster, DL, committed to Texas Tech

Jakari Lipsey, OT, committed to Michigan

David Gabriel Georges, RB, committed to Tennessee

Abraham Sesay, EDGE, committed to Notre Dame

Kamarui Dorsey, S, committed to Texas A&M

Oluwasemilore Olubobola, OT, committed to Notre Dame

Gideon Gash, ATH, committed to Texas Tech

Gabriel Osborne Jr., CB, committed to Oklahoma

Jacobs is in line to immediately become a key piece of Ohio State's defensive front after committing to the Buckeyes in Dec. 2025.

During his 2025 season at Blessed Trinity Catholic, he amassed 102 tackles, 24 tackles for loss and 16 sacks in 11 games (h/t 247Sports' Andrew Ivins ).

As for Matthews, it isn't hard to imagine him quickly becoming one of the SEC's top tackles once he joins Georgia.

He's listed at 6'5.5" and 300 pounds, as he's put together a dominant high school career at St. Thomas Aquinas in Florida. Matthews has also played basketball in high school, helping his team capture the Florida 6A title during his sophomore season.

David Gabriel Georges is the No. 2 running back in the latest prospect rankings, and it isn't hard to see why.

Georges helped Baylor School win the TSSAA Division II AAA state title last season, amassing 1,749 rush yards and 27 touchdowns on 161 carries during his junior year (h/t ESPN's Jason Jordan ).

He received offers from schools including Alabama, Auburn, Ohio State, Michigan and Oregon before choosing Tennessee.

articles.title: Two NJIC schools plan new football co-op; What it means and what's next
articles.summary: Administrators in Park Ridge and Emerson have expressed interest in joining forces for football starting in 2027.
articles.body:
Park Ridge and Emerson school districts have started the process of forming a cooperative sports football program for the 2027 season.

Park Ridge Superintendent Dr. Patrick Bernardo sent a letter to the community Nov. 17 saying while the agreement remains subject to North Jersey Interscholastic Conference (NJIC) approval and was not finalized, both districts had expressed mutual interest.

The two schools already co-op in multiple sports, including a successful wrestling program.

"This partnership represents an exciting opportunity to expand athletic opportunities for our students while continuing to build upon the positive relationship that already exists between our two communities," read a portion of the letter. "Emerson and Park Ridge have a longstanding history of working together through shared recreation programs, and this cooperative program reflects that same spirit of collaboration, community, and shared commitment to our students."

Emerson's final season as a single-entity football program was in 2022. It has partnered with Cresskill for the last three seasons, finishing 0-8 in 2026. That co-op was dissolved, giving Emerson the opportunity to find a new partner. Cresskill will likely seek a partner school to co-op in football moving forward.

The Park Ridge BOE passed a resolution for the district to enter into a football co-op at its latest meeting, while the Emerson BOE is expected to do the same at its meeting Nov. 23.

There will be a full membership meeting of the NJIC later this month, which needs to approve the partnership. Once it passes the conference, it will go before the New Jersey State Interscholastic Athletic Association (NJSIAA) cooperative sports committee, probably in January, for final ratifcation.

This is not the first time Park Ridge has sought a partnership with Emerson for football. The two schools attempted to co-op in 2022, but the full membership of the NJIC voted it down and so did the NJSIAA cooperative sports committee after an appeal. At the time, Park Ridge was coming off a 10-2 season and a North 1, Group 1 title.

Park Ridge has not had a winning season since it went 7-3 in 2023 and participation numbers at the school have flattened. The Owls finished 4-5 in 2026.

If approved, this would become the fifth football co-op in North Jersey, joining active programs Cliffside Park/Ridgefield, Palisades Park/Leonia and Waldwick/Midland Park. Waldwick/Midland Park won its first NJIC football championship in 2026.

A co-op for Harrison and North Arlington has been approved by the NJIC starting in 2027.

One school, likely Park Ridge, would be designated the Lead Local Educational Agency (LEA) and provide the bulk of the resources for the program, including being the primary location for practices and home games. Traditionally, co-op programs have rebranded with slight alterations to their uniforms and possibly nicknames to represent the change.

The ripple effect on schools and NJIC divisions

Back in 2022, the stated reason for turning down the partnership between the two schools was basically "they don't have to." Four years later, the need has grown and NJIC leadership expects this partnership to pass.

What happens to Cresskill football remains the next question. There have been discussions about Cresskill joining either Demarest or Tenafly for the 2027 season. Both of those schools currently play in the Ivy Division of the Super Football Conference.

Bogota is another program that may be looking to co-op starting in 2027. The Bucs had to shut down their program in the middle of the 2026 season, citing low numbers and player safety.

If Cresskill joins a school in the Super Football Conference, it would leave the conference with 24 football teams (if Bogota decides to remain a single entity). This past season the NJIC had three divisions with six teams and one with seven. The conference could decide to realign based on the number of schools and alter its popular conference championship format.

Hypothetically, it could have three eight-team divisions with all three division winners advancing to the semifinals along with one wild card team.

articles.title: Arsenal see THREE penalty VAR errors verdict reached by panel ahead of Premier League return
articles.summary: Arsenal have been on the receiving end of three wrong penalty decisions this season, the Key Match Incidents Panel has confirmed, covering incidents against...
articles.body:
Arsenal have been on the wrong end of THREE incorrect penalty calls this season, according to findings from a Key Match Incidents Panel. The Gunners secured a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Hull City in their final fixture before the November international break, courtesy of Martin Ødegaard's late intervention.

However, per the KMI Panel, Mikel Arteta's side should have been awarded an earlier opportunity from the spot. Just before the half-time whistle, Arsenal felt wronged when Nobel Mendy hauled back Kai Havertz inside the Tigers' penalty area.

Despite Arsenal being refused a penalty by referee Farai Hallam and VAR due to an offside position, the Panel have since voted 5:0 that the ruling was incorrect. A statement from the Panel read via The Mirror : "Although Havertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence by Havertz.

"Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded. The panel considered the VAR intervention was correct; however, the outcome after the on-field review was considered to be incorrect as a penalty should have been awarded."

Yet the Hull City incident is not the only contentious penalty call Arsenal have endured this campaign. The Gunners traveled to the Stadium of Light to face Sunderland AFC on September 12, coming away 2-0 victors thanks to second-half strikes from Bruno Guimarães and Bukayo Saka.

Earlier in the match, the Black Cats had an opportunity to open the scoring from the penalty spot, when Ezri Konsa dragged Dan Ballard to the turf during a corner. David Raya was there to produce one of the stops of the campaign so far, plunging low and powerfully to his left to thwart Enzo Le Fée from 12 yards.

However, the KMI Panel maintains that the spot kick should not have been awarded, due to Ballard also grappling with Konsa at the back post. A statement at the time read: "Although it was a very untidy challenge in which Konsa initially had arms around Ballard, Ballard engages in a holding action which pulls Konsa onto him so they both fall to the floor."

Finally, Arsenal benefited when a penalty was not given against them during their 1-0 victory over Liverpool at the start of the month. In comparable circumstances to Mendy's foul on Havertz, Jurriën Timber hauled back Alexander Isak in the area, but the Swede's protests were ignored.

To listen to the latest episode of 'All Out Soccer' - CLICK HERE

The KMI Panel believes 4:1 that Andy Madley should have granted a penalty to Liverpool, while a 3:2 vote indicated that VAR Stuart Attwell should have directed the official to the pitchside monitor for a review. They said: "The panel felt that a penalty should have been awarded for a holding action by Timber on Isak, 4:1.

"One panellist considered the short-lived holding to lack clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress. The majority also felt that VAR should have intervened to recommend an on-field review, 3:2, on the basis that it was a clear and obvious error. Two panellists considered that the subjectivity in assessing impact meant this did not meet the high threshold for VAR intervention."

Regardless of the rulings that have gone both in their favor and against them, Arsenal currently occupy top spot in the Premier League, sitting five points ahead of second-place Brighton and Hove Albion after 10 matches. The Gunners now shift their focus to an away fixture at Newcastle United on Saturday, November 21.

articles.title: Tashima open to meeting French rival over FIFA presidency bid
articles.summary: Kozo Tashima said on Wednesday he was prepared to hold talks with rival French candidate Philippe Diallo about their bids to become FIFA president.Diallo, th...
articles.body:
Kozo Tashima said on Wednesday he was prepared to hold talks with rival French candidate Philippe Diallo about their bids to become FIFA president.

The 68-year-old Tashima, who has served on the FIFA Council and is the Japan Football Association's honorary president, will attempt to unseat current FIFA chief Gianni Infantino in the March election.

Infantino is under pressure after his aborted plan to open up FIFA's premium competitions, such as the World Cup, to private investors.

Tashima said he wanted to make FIFA a "more trusted organisation" after Japan's FA officially submitted his candidacy for president of world football's governing body ahead of the Wednesday deadline.

Tashima also said he wanted to bring Japan's "strong sense of ethics" to football's top job.

Diallo, the president of the French Football Federation, was a late entrant to the race this week and has the backing of European football's governing body UEFA.

Tashima gave a cautious welcome to the Frenchman's suggestion of talks.

"Mr. Diallo has indicated that he wishes to speak with me. It's clear we need to talk," Tashima said in an interview with French sports daily L'Equipe.

"But we must consider one thing: is the mere fact that our programmes are similar, enough for us to decide to work together, or unite? Or should we think tactically, asking what the most effective strategy would be to defeat Infantino?"

Earlier, Tashima, who has served as a football player, coach and bureaucrat and has a reputation for being a safe pair of hands, set out the basis of his bid.

"We will share with the world the importance of fair play, respect and integrity -- the core values at the very heart of football and of sport itself," he said in a statement released by the JFA.

"With a strong sense of mission and firm resolve, I will take on this challenge so that FIFA can become a healthier and more trusted organisation and contribute even more to the further development of football worldwide."

In opposing Infantino, Tashima is going against his own confederation after the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) announced last month that it was backing Infantino for re-election.

Tashima was JFA president from 2016 to 2024 and also served on the AFC executive committee.

Infantino also has the backing of the Confederation of African Football (CAF), while South American governing body CONMEBOL is largely supportive.

Diallo said Tuesday he has support from countries beyond Europe.

Swiss former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega has also stated his intention to run for president.

Arsene Wenger, the French former Arsenal manager and FIFA's current chief of global football development, had at one point been seen as a potential candidate who could get Europe's backing but he will not stand.

The election will take place at the FIFA Congress on March 18 next year in the Moroccan capital, Rabat.

FIFA has a total of 211 member associations, with each having one vote in the presidential election.

articles.title: Georgia keeps winning, but Kirby Smart keeps worrying. There's a reason for that ...
articles.summary: While the college football world is full of chaos, the one constant is Kirby Smart and the Bulldogs.
articles.body:
Preseason college football predictions in the best of times are coin-flips; preseason predictions in a catastrophe-ridden year like this one are unintentionally hilarious. Ohio State's going to win another natty! LSU is headed to the playoff! This is Oregon's year! Pretty much every preseason favorite has sputtered, stalled or spun into the ground at one time or another this season.

The Georgia Bulldogs just keep on winning — with one inexplicable exception, but we'll get to that — and winning in a way that leaves no doubt about their dominance. Check the numbers: except for the narrow 20-17 win over CFP No. 3 Alabama, Georgia has won its other eight games by at least 19 points.

And after that three-point loss to Auburn in October, a game in Georgia's hands until the final seconds, the Dawgs dropped a combined 117 points on their next three opponents, all ranked, allowing Florida, Ole Miss and Missouri to score only a combined 36.

All of this is a testament to the remarkable consistency that Kirby Smart has imposed on this program. It's tough to remember now, but before Smart, Georgia was a generational underachiever, capable of winning double-digit games in a season but never the ones that mattered most. A long, dark four decades passed between the Dawgs' last championship in 1980 and the back-to-back ones under Smart in 2021 and 2022.

Now, Smart has the red-and-black battle station fully operational. Georgia has been in the national championship conversation every season for a decade. This year, Georgia is one win from a guaranteed berth in the SEC championship, which would be the Bulldogs' ninth appearance in the past 10 conference title games.

Only a ranked-but-wobbly South Carolina and a deeply overmatched Georgia Tech remain on Georgia's slate. After that, the Dawgs could well get a first-round bye regardless of how the final conference title game plays out. And from there, well … who knows, but Georgia's consistency fits the playoff a whole lot better than the chaotic energy of virtually every other school in the bracket.

At this point, the real challenge to Georgia isn't from Alabama or Utah or Notre Dame. The most serious threat to the Bulldogs might be already inside their stadium. It might be on their roster. It might be looking back at them from the mirror. The Bulldogs' greatest threat might just be themselves, is what I'm getting at here.

Smart spent eight seasons at Alabama under Nick Saban before taking over Georgia in 2016, and you can see Saban's crushing-defense, no-BS influence in Smart's style. Like Saban before him, Smart has managed to keep meddling and cranky boosters in line.

You watch Georgia, and you see a fearsome juggernaut. But listen to what Smart says about his team, and you'll start to hear some fascinating comments. This isn't the usual talking-up-the-cupcake-opponent speech; Smart spends his time at the podium airing real frustrations and giving us a look at his psyche in a rapidly evolving college sports landscape.

After the Missouri win, a thundering victory in which he was nonetheless bellowing at his players even while up big , Smart noted that he would like to see the players holding one another more accountable than he believes Georgia — or anyone — is now.

"The best teams I've been on, they had guys ready to kick somebody's ass on the sideline because of the same things I saw [during the game]," he said on Saturday . "So the player-led version I'm seeing now is like a millennial player-led, because 10 years ago, it would have been player-led." (Smart means Gen Z, not millennial; any team still fielding millennial players in their 30s and 40s would not be making the College Football Playoff.)

"I don't think in this day and age, more kids want to confront and demand each other," Smart continued. "So if they're not willing to, then I'll volunteer." It's the latest of many comments Smart has made over the years about players getting too comfortable and not demanding enough of themselves or each other.

And this is where the dark clouds gather for Georgia fans. Saban retired in January 2024, and one of his stated reasons — in addition to his age — was the changing power dynamic between players and coaches.

"I thought we could have a hell of a team [in 2024] and then maybe 70 or 80 percent of the players you talk to, all they want to know is two things: 'What assurances do I have that I'm going to play,' because they're thinking about transferring, and 'How much are you going to pay me?'" Saban said in 2024 shortly after he retired . "So I'm saying to myself, 'Maybe this doesn't work anymore, that the goals and aspirations are just different and that it's all about how much money can I make as a college player?' I'm not saying that's bad. I'm not saying it's wrong, I'm just saying that's never been what we were all about, and it's not why we had success through the years."

It's worth pointing out that Smart has, in fact, had considerable success in the NIL era, and has managed to navigate it — often at Saban's expense — in a way few others have managed. Smart has said he's not against players being paid, and has joked he wished he had that opportunity when he was playing, but noted earlier this season that paying players can have downstream effects that don't benefit the team as much as the player's bank account.

"I think about the teams we had in '21 and '22, and how physical they were and how they practiced. We can't even get close to that now," Smart said after Georgia's Halloween decimation of Florida. "If it's a different culture that guys don't want to as much, I don't know. They were definitely hungrier, because there was a motivation to make it. A lot of these guys, honestly, they make more than I did until I was 40. It's just a different day and age."

Whether you agree with Saban and Smart that college players are too NIL-focused, or believe players are receiving appropriate compensation for their labor, isn't really the central issue here; the question is how much more of this Smart is willing to put up with before he decides to hang up the visor. That could be several decades in the future — Smart is 50, Saban was 72 when he retired — or it could come a lot sooner than that.

Before then, though, Georgia has a few important games to play, perhaps even late into January. The Bulldogs will be favored in most, if not all, of them … because no matter how the bracket shakes out, Georgia won't have to face Georgia. Yet.
